study_identification_part.si4_title: A 10-Year Longitudinal Study of Brain Cortical Thickness in People with First-Episode Psychosis Using Normative Models

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To map the associations between brain cortical abnormalities and clinical symptoms over the long term (approximately 10 years) in people with first-episode schizophrenia spectrum psychosis using normative modeling. To assess whether individual differences in cortical deviations would be coupled to clinical outcomes over time.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Hierarchical Bayesian Regression (HBR) with scanner ID as batch effect; HBR fits site-specific intercepts and slopes to accommodate inter-site variation; Transfer learning used to adapt pre-trained normative models from 77 sites to 3 unseen Oslo scanners using local controls; Covariates preserved: age (fixed effect), sex (batch effect)
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: To account for site and scanner effects, we used the Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) approach for normative modeling, which efficiently accommodates inter-site variation and provides computational scaling, which is useful for multi-cohort and longitudinal studies with data from different scanners. We estimated a normative model for each region of interest (ROI, n = 150) in the Freesurfer Destrieux atlas, using HBR with age as a covariate, and sex and scanner id as batch effects, to predict CT. This accommodated multisite pooling using transfer learning and comparisons across scanners... We then adapted the model to the 3 unseen Oslo scanners, by transferring the (hyper) parameters as informed priors for these new sites... Importantly, as HBR fits site-specific intercepts and slopes, the resulting normative trajectory might not be linear across the lifespan, but rather piecewise linear... Figure 1 displays the joint distributions of the median CT and their associated deviation scores for all healthy CTRL from the validation set of the adaptation (transfer) dataset. Of interest are the marginal densities: normative modeling of the median CT accounting for site and sex aligns the distributions and allows meaningful comparisons between samples from different sites in the deviation scores space.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear mixed effects (LME) models to test effects of diagnosis, time since inclusion, age at baseline, sex, and diagnosis×time interaction on deviation scores across 150 ROIs, with subject-specific random intercepts; FDR correction (Benjamini-Hochberg, α=0.05) for multiple comparisons across ROIs; Non-parametric Wilcoxon tests for case-control differences in proportion of extreme deviations at each timepoint; LME models to assess change in PANSS subscales over time (controlling for age and sex); LME models to test associations between deviation scores in different ROIs and PANSS domain scores (total, positive, negative, general), including time×deviation interaction effects; Mann-Whitney U tests and χ² tests for attrition analyses
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: First-episode psychosis patients showed diffuse cortical thickness reductions at baseline that attenuated over 10 years together with symptom reduction, inconsistent with a simple neurodegenerative model of schizophrenia.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: LME models revealed significant conditional main effects of diagnosis and time×diagnosis interactions in a distributed cortical network encompassing bilateral temporal, parietal, and frontal regions, where negative deviations in patients (Cohen's d=-0.46 at baseline, -0.43 at 12 months, -0.27 at 10 years) attenuated over time. At baseline and 12-month follow-up, patients showed significantly higher proportions of extreme negative deviations (P=2.56×10⁻⁵ and P=.0006, respectively), but no significant differences at 10-year follow-up (P=1). PANSS scores significantly decreased over time (P<.001), with main improvements during the first year. LME models revealed associations between cortical deviations and PANSS scores: anterior cingulate gyrus was associated with PANSS total (coefficient=-4.0, P=.003) and PANSS general (coefficient=-1.79, P=.01); left anterior segment of circular sulcus of insula (coefficient=-1.3, P=.04), posterior ramus of lateral sulcus (coefficient=1.52, P=.03), and medial orbital sulcus (coefficient=-1.42, P=.02) were associated with PANSS negative. A significant time×deviation interaction was found for the left posterior ramus of lateral sulcus on PANSS negative scores (coefficient=0.28, P=.047), indicating initial associations attenuated over time. Medication use showed primarily second-generation antipsychotics (62% at baseline, 48% at 12 months, 17% at 10 years) or no antipsychotics (38%, 50%, 83%, respectively). No significant differences in attrition were found for healthcare contacts, PANSS scores, or median cortical deviation scores.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Moderate sample size at 10-year follow-up (n=23 patients, n=77 controls) may have reduced power at later timepoints, though retention rates compare favorably to literature; inability to directly test differential effects of first- vs second-generation antipsychotics due to very small number on first-generation drugs; extreme cortical deviations may relate to factors beyond schizophrenia pathology (noise, artifacts, medications, co-morbidities, lifestyle factors); different scanners across waves may have influenced findings despite normative modeling validation; representative recruitment challenges in clinical cohorts; lack of information from important neurodevelopmental phases prevents direct inference about neurodevelopmental antecedents
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Finally, we acknowledge that our sample size at the third follow-up session is moderate, and this reduction in sample size could have biased our findings at later timepoints... Second, whilst our findings are suggestive that second-generation antipsychotics may have different chronic effects on brain structure to first-generation antipsychotics, we were unable to test this directly because only a very small number of participants were taking first-generation antipsychotics in our sample... Third, extreme cortical deviations may not only relate to schizophrenia-related pathologies but could also be markers of other effects, e.g., noise, artifacts, medications, co-morbidities, co-existing conditions, and various lifestyle and health-related behaviors or traits... the inclusion of different scanners across different waves of the study may have influenced our findings... ensuring representative recruitment in clinical and population-based cohorts is nontrivial, e.g., inclusion and exclusion criteria of patients or bias on the selection of healthy subjects or the retention of individuals with psychosis and CTRL... we emphasize that our data cannot inform directly about the neurodevelopmental antecedents of schizophrenia because we lack information from important neurodevelopmental phases.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Transfer learning approach allowed meaningful comparisons across different scanners over 10-year longitudinal period; Norwegian National Registry data used to validate against attrition bias by tracking healthcare contacts for all patients; Sex-stratified effects and age-by-diagnosis interactions were examined; Spin permutation tests applied for spatial correlations of effect maps; Medication information collected at each timepoint showing shift from antipsychotic use to no medication over time

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is one of the longest prospective longitudinal neuroimaging studies of first-episode psychosis (10-year follow-up) using modern normative modeling approaches. The study demonstrates practical application of transfer learning from large-scale multi-site reference models (77 sites, N≈40,435) to local clinical cohorts with different scanners. The attenuation of cortical deviations over time is particularly notable given that most patients were on second-generation antipsychotics, contrasting with older studies using first-generation antipsychotics. The high proportion of patients no longer on medication at 10-year follow-up (83%) reflects clinical recovery trajectories. Retention rates: patients 85% at 12 months, 38% at 10 years (from 12-month sample); controls 90% at 12 months, 35% at 10 years. The study period spanned multiple scanner transitions (1.5T Siemens Sonata → 3T GE HDxT → 3T GE 750 Discovery) without temporal overlap, demonstrating robustness of HBR normative modeling approach. The reference normative models included only first-visit data when multiple visits were available in the publicly available datasets.
